abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Chemotherapy and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are widely utilized in cancer treatment, exerting not only direct cytotoxic effects on tumor cells but also significantly reshaping the systemic immune status of patients, particularly the composition and function of the T cell repertoire. This review begins with the analysis of the widespread depletion and dysfunction of early T cell subsets in cancer patients, particularly naïve T cells (Tn) and stem-like memory T cells (Tscm). Afterward, it details how chemotherapy and ICIs differentially regulate T cell homeostasis, including their ability to induce T cell exhaustion and differentiation skewing, as well as their ability to stimulate immunity and remodel the tumor microenvironment. On this basis, it is shown that the quality of T cell memory phenotypes is central in determining the in vivo expansion and persistence of chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cells. To overcome the challenges of classical autologous CAR-T therapy, which stems from raw material quality and in vitro manufacturing bottlenecks, we focus on transforming chemotherapy and ICIs from traditional treatment modalities into beneficial “host preconditioning” regimens aimed at optimizing the baseline state of the endogenous T cell repertoire. All in all, this transformation of traditional therapies into host preconditioning strategies, along with recent advances in in vivo CAR-T approaches, provides theoretical grounds and translatable clues to develop next-generation cellular immunotherapy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) therapy has been effective in the treatment of hematologic malignancies in patients. Yet, its effectiveness continues to be limited in solid tumors and in patients who have undergone several lines of therapy [1,2]. Growing evidence suggests that pre-treatment status of host T-cells, such as differentiation stage, memory phenotype, and functional integrity, significantly affects in vivo expansion capacity, persistence, and eventual clinical efficacy of CAR-T cells [1,3,4].

Chemotherapy and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are the main strategies for treating tumors and have an important impact on the immune microenvironment of patients [5,6]. Chemotherapy is known to cause T cell exhaustion, decreasing their frequency and functional status, especially resulting in the depletion of naïve T cells (Tn) and stem-like memory T cells (Tscm). This depletion severely restricts subsequent CAR-T cell manufacturing and therapeutic efficacy [5,6]. Notably, chemotherapy and ICIs show substantial immunomodulatory potential, as chemotherapy can induce antitumor immunity by causing immunogenic cell death and removing immunosuppressive cells [7,8], whereas ICIs can reverse T cell exhaustion and enhance T cell function and memory formation [9]. This “remodeling” effect on the immune system, rather than mere “suppression”, offers robust scientific reasons to use them along with in vivo CAR-T therapy.

To optimize CAR-T therapy, we must go beyond the traditional cytotoxic perspective and develop comprehensive dialectical knowledge of the chemotherapy and ICIs’ double-edged effect on the T-cell repertoire. This review aims to systematically summarize the underlying mechanisms, focusing on transforming conventional “destructive” treatments into beneficial “preconditioning” strategies. This therefore provides a theoretical framework and translational pathway for the generation of next-generation in vivo CAR-T therapies.

sec.title: Memory T cell biology and its alterations in cancer patients
Phenotype and function of memory T cells
sec.p: Memory T cells are fundamental executors of adaptive immunity and serve as carriers of long-lasting immunological memory. Their functional status directly influences the intensity and durability of the body's anti-tumor immune response [10]. Memory T cells can be categorized into multiple subsets that form a continuous spectrum based on differentiation stages, homing characteristics, and functional preferences [11]. Collectively, these subsets constitute the immunological cornerstone for defending against tumor recurrence and metastasis [10].

Based on their functional and phenotypic characteristics, T lymphocytes can be classified into two primary categories: Tn and memory T cells [10,11]. Tn cells are the precursor of immune responses. Following the recognition of antigen presentations by dendritic cells, they become activated and initiate a complex differentiation programme. This process typically follows a progressive pathway, transitioning from Tn to stem cell-like memory T cells (Tscm), then to central memory T cells (Tcm), effector memory T cells (Tem), and ultimately to terminally differentiated effector T cells (Teff) [10,12]. As T cells differentiate, their fate becomes more restricted. They gradually lose their self-renewal and pluripotency capacities and gain more immediate effector functions. During this process, the expression of homing receptors, such as CD62L (L-selectin) and CC-chemokine receptor 7 (CCR7), undergoes dynamic changes. These receptors are predominantly expressed on specific subsets, including Tn, early-Tscm, and Tcm, which determines their ability to participate in lymphocyte recirculation [12,13]. During the primary immune response, only a small percentage (5–10%) of the activated T cells become differentiated into long-lived memory T cells [12,13]. These memory T cells not only persist long-term in the body and retain self-renewal capacity but also mount rapid and potent responses upon re-exposure to antigens.

Among the memory T cells, Tscm is prominent because of their long lifespan, robust self-renewal capability, and potential for multiple differentiation [10]. Recognized as the “fountainhead” of the memory T cell pool, Tscm continuously replenishes more differentiated subsets, such as Tcm and Tem, thereby serving as the cornerstone for maintaining long-term immune surveillance and responsiveness [10]. Thymic involution occurs naturally with aging, leading to lower output of Tn and Tscm. However, the memory T cell compartment remains diverse and plastic, allowing the generation of T cells specific for new pathogens and tumors [14]. The maintenance of this important function depends on the balancing of generation, survival, and apoptosis of memory T cell populations. When this equilibrium is disturbed, immune exhaustion, antigen non-responsiveness, and other pathological states occur [15]. Memory T-cells are not only the biological basis for immunological memory, but their quantity, phenotype, and functional quality are important readouts, as well as key determinants in the design and assessment of all T-cell-based immunotherapies, especially the adoptive cell therapies [1,3,4].

sec.title: Early exhaustion of the naïve and stem-like memory T cell pool in cancer patients
sec.p: Substantial evidence suggests that the T-cell immune landscape is markedly remodeled in cancer patients upon first diagnosis, and this remodeling does not appear to simply reflect age. A distinct feature of this phenomenon is the early and sustained lack of Tn and Tscm [5]. The major importance of these findings relates to their universality and clinical relevance. Patients with solid tumors like rhabdomyosarcoma and neuroblastoma, and those with hematologic malignancies such as acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), and Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) have a significantly lower percentage and absolute counts of Tn and Tscm in their peripheral blood than that of corresponding healthy controls [5,[16], [17], [18]]. Moreover, this decline is much greater than what one would think age can cause. In subjects with advanced non-small cell lung carcinoma, the absolute counts of all Tn and Tm subsets were significantly lower than those of healthy controls [13]. The depletion of CD4+/CD8+ Tn and CD8+ Tscm subsets exhibited significant correlations with disease stage, tumor metastasis, and shorter progression-free survival (PFS), indicating their important clinical prognostic value [13].

The mechanisms underlying this early deficiency are complex and arise from multifactorial interactions. An essential element is first the failure of thymic output [19]. For example, at diagnosis, ALL patients show markedly reduced thymic output that does not recover over the long term. As a consequence of this condition, there is inadequate replenishment of the naïve T cell pool, and the absolute counts of memory-phenotype CD4+ and CD8+ T cells are greatly decreased [20,21]. The tumor microenvironment actively suppresses immune responses through specific mechanisms [5,17]. Tumor-derived microvesicles, for example, can preferentially activate apoptosis in CD8+ T cells via the Fas/Fas ligand pathway while causing expansion in regulatory T cells (Tregs) [5,17]. Subsequently, this process enhances immunosuppression. Moreover, cancer can cause systemic disruption of the lymphocyte homeostasis, which leads to decreased lymphocyte production and increased apoptosis. This also explains why the absolute lymphocyte count serves as a robust prognostic indicator for various malignancies [[22], [23], [24], [25]].

As pivotal cells in initiating immune responses against antigens, the early depletion of Tn and Tscm hinders patients from establishing effective de novo immune responses and durable immune memory. This deficiency could be a major mechanism underlying the generation of refractory tumors and immune evasion [13,26]. More importantly, the depletion of this “seed cell reservoir” fundamentally undermines the foundation of adoptive cell therapies, such as CAR-T. If the host does not have sufficient quantity and quality of Tn and Tscm cells with strong proliferative potential and plasticity, any further attempt to manufacture CAR-T cells ex vivo or generate them in vivo will face the challenge of “lacking the necessary resources for production [4].” Hence, the future therapeutic strategies aimed at reconstructing and expanding the naïve cell reservoir are expected to fundamentally improve the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy by providing new opportunities to improve the efficacy of cell therapies [27].

sec.title: Reshaping the T cell repertoire: effects of chemotherapy
Overall dynamics: lymphodepletion, reconstitution, and long-term shifts in T cell compartment
sec.p: The impact of chemotherapy on the T-cell repertoire is a dynamically evolving process that can be broadly summarized into three interrelated stages: rapid lymphodepletion, unbalanced immune reconstitution, and ultimately, long-term compositional and functional skewing of the T-cell compartment [5,28]. This dynamic process highlights the intrinsic nature of chemotherapy-induced long-term effects on the host immune system.

Lymphopenia or reduction in lymphocyte count level is seen in nearly every patient with any major disease, whether hematological malignancy or solid organ tumor, due to chemotherapy [5,21,28,29]. Lymphocyte damage usually worsens as therapy severity intensifies. However, the recovery kinetics of different lymphocyte subsets are fundamentally different [14,19,28,30,31]. The process of reconstitution that is not balanced causes long-term pathological reorganization of the T cell repertoire, which is characterized by a long-term depletion of Tn and Tscm. In addition, there is a global shift in the memory T cell pool toward more differentiated phenotypes [5,32]. Most chemotherapy regimens, regardless of the cancer type, will cause a lasting depletion of Tn cells [5,33,34]. Interestingly, chemotherapy not only causes T cell exhaustion at an early lineage stage. Also, it activates the immune system, increases profiles, and differentiates T cells while decreasing Tn cells [32]. Moreover, certain patients may present with a Tn deficiency before chemotherapy [5]. This congenital immune defect can be worsened by chemotherapy, thus limiting further application of immunotherapy treatment [5]. While regenerating this imbalance is further manifested by a relative enrichment of antigen-experienced memory cells, and poor replenishment of naïve nascent cells. In this context, a lower clonal diversity in the T-cell repertoire and “aged” differentiation state overall emerges [20,32].

In conclusion, chemotherapy exerts a long-term influence on the T-cell repertoire, beyond the short-term numerical decline observed during treatment. Altering the homeostatic regeneration processes can impart long-lasting and maybe irreversible T cell differentiation bias as well as loss of functional potential [5,21,28,29]. This “legacy effect” may lead to a direct depletion of high-quality T-cell raw materials that are essential for adoptive cell therapy [32]. Thus, the chemotherapy history of the patient should be treated as one of the major factors when designing CAR-T treatment strategies, especially those involving in vivo CAR-T approaches relying on host endogenous T cells.

sec.title: Disparate effects on major T cell subsets: CD4+/CD8+ T cells and memory subsets
sec.p: Chemotherapy exerts fundamentally distinct effects on CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, as well as their respective memory subsets, which dictate the kinetics and ultimate pattern of T-cell immune reconstitution following chemotherapy (Table 1). Particularly, CD8+ T cells as well as natural killer (NK) cell populations recover rapidly, whereas B cells and CD4+ T cells (especially naïve CD4+ T cells) recover slowly and often incompletely for several years [14,19,28,30,31]. The difference stems from the different pathways of regeneration of CD8+ and CD4+ T cells. The expansion of peripheral memory cells is the principal contributor to CD8+ T cells, which allows faster recovery [35]. In contrast, the regeneration of the CD4+T cell pool, especially of the naïve pool, is very much dependent on the thymic output function and age-related. The process of reconstitution presents unique difficulties for adults and the elderly [19,36]. As a result, the essential differences in the regenerative mechanisms are that CD4+ T cells, especially the naïve subset, are more susceptible and less resilient [20,31,37,38], while CD8+ T cells recover more quickly [35].

sec.p: The CD4+ T cell pool is particularly vulnerable to chemotherapy. High-dose chemotherapy can result in a substantial decrease of over 60% in the total number of CD4+ T cells, with a notably severe decline of up to 90% or more in the naïve (CD45RA+) subset. This condition of depletion may last for many years [37]. As a result of aging-related thymic dysfunction, CD4+ T cell regeneration is vigorous in children, but adult and older patients often suffer from persistent deficiencies, particularly in the naïve subset [19,30]. Moreover, the effects of various chemotherapy regimens show considerable heterogeneity. For example, temozolomide, docetaxel, and adjuvant radio-chemotherapy regimen are associated with long-term depletion of CD4+ T cells [28,38,39]. The cisplatin/gemcitabine/fluorouracil regimen administered for pancreatic cancer, on the other hand, shows a temporarily elevated proportion of CD4+ T cells [40]. This shows that various chemotherapy regimens have a differential effect on CD4+ T cells.

In comparison to CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells exhibit greater resilience during recovery. Their regeneration primarily depends on the expansion of pre-existing memory cells located in the periphery, particularly the Tem subset [35,41,42]. The effective doubling time is shorter, meaning baseline restoration may occur within months of treatment [35,41]. The treatment often leads to an increase in Tem cells and a decrease in terminally differentiated effector cells during therapy for several cancers, like glioblastoma and lung cancer [38,43]. Although high-dose agents, such as cyclophosphamide and platinum-based drugs, may lead to declines in CD8+ T cell counts, the overall kinetics and magnitude of their recovery generally surpass those of CD4+ T cells [29,44]. Interestingly, low-dose cyclophosphamide may even induce a transient elevation of CD8+ T cell levels [29,44,45].

The fundamental differences in the regeneration pathways of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells contribute to a long-term imbalance in the CD4+/CD8+ ratio of the T cell repertoire following chemotherapy [28,35,41,46]. Due to chemotherapy, less-differentiated T cells are selectively depleted, resulting in the imbalance [5,29,32,41]. As an example, after chemotherapy in individuals with B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (B-NHL), the proportion of Tn decreases, but the proportion of Tem rises. In addition, single-cell sequencing has established decreased clonal diversity of T cells, along with a shift to a more differentiated state [32]. In ALL patients, pre-existing T-cell deficiencies at diagnosis synergistically interact with chemotherapy, resulting in thymic output and naïve T-cell proportions consistently lower than those of healthy controls. Meanwhile, the remaining T-cell pool becomes enriched with antigen-experienced memory T cells [20].

sec.title: Functional and metabolic impairment of T cells
sec.p: Chemotherapy not only reduces the number and alters the phenotype of T cells, but more worryingly, it functionally dysregulates T cells long-term and damages their metabolic foundations [47]. This may make the patient's T cells “non-functional” or “unfit” for adoptive cell therapy.

Chemotherapy is known to induce a programmed dysregulation of T cells at the molecular level with negative transcriptional and epigenetic reprogramming. This condition will change the state of T cells and transition them from an activated/survival state to an exhausted/dysfunctional state [32,48]. For example, T cells of patients with B-NHL show upregulated pro-exhaustion genes (e.g., galectin 1 [LGALS1]) and downregulated pro-survival genes (e.g., human immunodeficiency virus type I enhancer binding protein 2 [HIVEP2]) after chemotherapy. These changes are accompanied by DNA methylation alterations that are linked to functional decline and could lock T cells into a permanently dysfunctional state [32,48]. As a result, T cell functional potential is generally impaired due to dysregulation at the molecular level. In clinical practice, this phenomenon refers to the reduced in vitro expansion potential of T cells with increased chemotherapy cycles. Research into pediatric oncology shows that the capacity of T-cells to expand widely varies across different types of cancer, such as ALL, non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL), and solid tumors [5]. At diagnosis, standard-risk ALL (SR-ALL) patients exhibit the highest expansion capacity; however, this capacity sharply declines during chemotherapy. On the other hand, the NHL and most solid tumor patients usually have lower baseline expansion [5]. In vitro experiments confirm that chemotherapeutic agents doxorubicin and cytarabine completely inhibit T-cell proliferation [5,47]. In particular, even T-cells that barely survive chemotherapy often exhibit “functional fragility,” characterized by abnormal sensitivity to restimulation, increased susceptibility to activation-induced cell death (AICD), and diminished magnitude and rate of expansion [5,47].

The mechanism for the above-mentioned functional impairment may be attributed to severe damage to mitochondrial function, which particularly affects Tn [47]. Research indicates that cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and cytarabine cause Tn to show a significantly greater impairment of mitochondrial function parameters (e.g., oxygen consumption rate [OCR], extracellular acidification rate [ECAR], and spare respiratory capacity [SRC]) than Tcm and Tem [47]. Various drugs have very different mechanisms of action. For example, cyclophosphamide induces broad mitochondrial damage in all T-cell subsets (including Tn, Tcm, and Tem) as shown by reduced volume, decrease in membrane potential, and dampened ability to respond to stress. Cytarabine leads to sustained and severe metabolic damage in all T-cell subsets. On the contrary, doxorubicin effects are largely reversible upon stimulating the cells [47]. Clinical sample analysis further confirmed that chemotherapy induces abnormal morphological changes in T cells, including mitochondrial miniaturization and disruption of cristae structures [47]. Damage to the “cellular power plants” directly impairs the energy supply and metabolic adaptability essential for T cell activation and long-term proliferation. Furthermore, it specifically undermines the functional basis of naïve and early memory T cells, which are the long-term regenerative populations.

These findings together explain that the T-cell products obtained from chemotherapy patients perform poorly at the transcriptional, epigenetic, and metabolic levels [32,48,49]. Clinical evidence has also confirmed that patients who do not respond tend to have increased levels of expression of exhaustion and terminal differentiation markers in their pre-infusion T cells or manufactured CAR-T products [50,51]. Therefore, it is important to understand and overcome these obstacles to improve the cell therapy strategy.

sec.title: Balancing dose and regimen: toward optimal immunomodulation
sec.p: Indeed, the preceding discourse demonstrated the effects of chemotherapy on T-cell homeostasis. It showed that while chemotherapy induces lymphocyte depletion and creates immunological space, it may also exhaust early-lineage T cells, produce dysfunction, and cause epigenetic malfunction (Table 1) [32,47,48]. All in all, these observations lead to a major conundrum: how to achieve an optimal dose and intensity of chemotherapy that maximizes preconditioning benefits (elimination of immunosuppressive cells, upregulation of homeostatic cytokines, etc) and minimizes irreversible damage to the endogenous T-cell repertoire?

Unfortunately, few systematic studies evaluate the actual contribution of chemotherapy dose and intensity on memory T cells [20,38]. The current literature focuses on examining qualitative differences between chemotherapy regimens in terms of T cell repertoire shaping [47,[52], [53], [54]]. However, there is a lack of robust data estimating the dose-response relationship between intensity gradients and T cell protection or damage. The main reason for this gap can be attributed in part to the complex nature of dose effects, which hampers easy extrapolation for optimization. A chemotherapeutic agent may have opposite immunomodulatory effects at different doses. For instance, low-dose cyclophosphamide can specifically deplete Tregs and promote anti-tumor immune responses [55]; high-dose cyclophosphamide will cause extensive lymphocyte depletion and T-cell dysfunction [29,44]. Managing this non-linear relationship is the crux of dose optimization. Furthermore, unique factors interplay to create very patient-relevant dose windows; for instance, tumour type, age, baseline immune status, and treatments before, as well as combinations thereof, could be considered for the realization of ideal dose windows. For example, as the thymus is active in a pediatric patient and has a high T-cell regeneration capacity, a pediatric patient can tolerate higher cumulative lymphodepleting chemotherapy doses without permanent damage [19,30]. In contrast, elderly patients or patients with severely depleted T-cell reserves who have already undergone multiple lines of therapy may suffer irreversible injury even at standard doses [35,56,57]. The study design limitations are also significant. Dynamic monitoring of T cell subsets is mostly earmarked as exploratory in most clinical trials utilizing various antitumor efficacy as endpoints. Due to their small sample sizes and insufficient dose groups, it is challenging to identify dose-response relationships in these studies. Moreover, discrepancies in T-cell subset detection methods between studies impede data integration and comparison.

Moving forward with the actual scenario, future research regarding the patient must focus on several directions related to the breakthroughs. Clinical trials on dose-finding in the future must be planned to establish multiple dose groups under fixed chemotherapy regimens in order to systematically look at the effect of different doses on the quantity, function, and transcriptome of T cell subsets, particularly Tscm and Tcm. Secondly, predictive biomarkers should be established, including baseline T cell phenotype, thymic output function, and mitochondrial quality, to guide individualized dose selection [4,32]. At the same time, dynamic monitoring should be implemented to assess the change of T cells at multiple time points—before and after lymphodepletion, before CAR-T infusion, and after CAR-T infusion—to promptly adjust the next treatment [4,32]. In the end, a preclinical model should be used to explore the dose-dependent immune modulation mechanism to provide a basis for clinical transformation.

In short, optimizing chemotherapy dose may be a key component of “precision preconditioning,” but this is an area of early development. The future efforts will likely establish patient-specific dosage decision systems having a better understanding of T-cell kinetics and the mechanisms that regulate immune homeostasis. This development can change chemotherapy from a “double-edged sword” to a mere immunomodulator.

sec.title: Reshaping the T cell repertoire by immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs)
Enhanced memory T cell function and formation by ICIs monotherapy
sec.p: In contrast to the potential depletion and damage of T cells caused by chemotherapy, the ICIs therapy mainly works to release the intrinsic inhibition of T cells, thereby reversing exhaustion and reshaping the T cell repertoire (Table 2) [60]. In the course of this remodeling process, the expansion and functional improvement of memory T-cell subsets represent a key step linked with durable antitumor immune responses and clinical benefit [9,61,62].
