sec.p: Memory T cells can get enhanced in their size, function, and tissue distribution through rich molecular pathways with the help of programmed cell death-1/programmed cell death-ligand 1 (PD-1/PD-L1) inhibitors like pembrolizumab and nivolumab. Pembrolizumab can expand the CD8+ Tem and Teff of patients with Sézary syndrome, while inducing a substantial increase in the number of intratumoral CD8+ memory T cells [9], along with a reduced frequency of CD4+ Tem [61]. In sebaceous carcinoma, circulating central memory and effector memory phenotype CD8+ T cells and mature CD16+CD57+ NK cells are associated with the efficacy of pembrolizumab [63]. Enrichment of peripheral memory T cells and NK cells may lead to the response [63]. The presence of high-frequency CD103+PD-1+CD8+ T cells, displaying a central memory phenotype, is linked to improved PFS in advanced gastric cancer treatment with nivolumab [64]. This suggests that differentiation towards an effector memory phenotype may correlate with treatment response. Furthermore, the enrichment of CD103+CD8+ tissue-resident memory T cells (Trm) is closely linked to nivolumab treatment response and enhanced survival in patients with esophageal cancer [65]. Additional studies indicate that nivolumab can systematically activate the Tem and Tcm subsets of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in patients with malignant melanoma, thereby promoting Th1 polarization [66]. In patients with non-small cell lung cancer and melanoma, a higher ratio of Tcm to Teff is associated with prolonged PFS [26]. Meanwhile, studies have demonstrated that non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients who respond to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade frequently show a higher proportion of naïve and memory CD4+ T cells with cytokine secretion capabilities [67]. These patients also tend to exhibit improved gut microbiota diversity and characteristics associated with peripheral memory T cells and NK cells [68]. Similar preclinical studies have confirmed that serplulimab effectively increases the proportion of effector and memory T cells within the tumor microenvironment while simultaneously reducing the number of Tregs [69].

Cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4) inhibitors are also efficacious at remodeling the memory T cell pool. Ipilimumab, for example, is capable of inducing a systemic rise in the central-to-effector memory T cell ratio [70]. Simultaneously, it decreases Tn in individuals with myeloid malignancies while enhancing memory T cell populations and increasing the expression of related activation and co-stimulatory markers [71]. In melanoma patients who responded to ipilimumab treatment, higher frequencies of CD8+ Tem positively correlated with better survival rates. Moreover, this agent reduces the number of suppressive populations, including Tregs and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) [62]. Further analysis showed that baseline numbers of CD45RO+CD8+ T cells, as well as the naïve/memory T cell ratio, possessed intrinsic predictive value in melanoma patients treated with ipilimumab [72,73].

These findings suggest that an equilibrium favoring a memory phenotype is an important immunological basis for the effectiveness of ICIs [61,62]. This mechanistic insight strongly supports the use of ICI as preconditioning for the generation of CAR-T cells in vivo. By administering ICI before CAR-T production in vivo, the host endogenous T-cell repertoire is optimized.

sec.title: Synergistic reshaping of the T cell repertoire by ICIs combination strategies
sec.p: The use of combination ICI therapy can provide greater clinical benefits than monotherapy through simultaneous alleviation of a range of inhibitory signals on T cell activation. It promotes clonal proliferation and augments the functions of memory T cell subsets (Table 2) [74,75]. The combination of ICI dual therapy, like nivolumab plus ipilimumab, has beneficial effects on multiple tumor types. For example, this combination treatment produces a higher rate of pathological response than monotherapy in the neoadjuvant treatment of resectable non-small cell lung cancer and substantially increases the frequency of Tem and Trm [76]. In patients with melanoma, those who respond to treatment show an enrichment of EOMES+CD69+CD45RO+ Tem cells within the tumors that correlates with a reduction in tumour volume and PFS [74]. In malignant pleural mesothelioma, durvalumab plus tremelimumab mobilizes CD57+ Tem into circulation, induces intratumoral tertiary lymphoid structures, induces both systemic and local anti-tumor immunity, and associates with clinical benefit [75]. Additional research on hepatocellular carcinoma patients receiving atezolizumab plus bevacizumab suggests that dynamic changes of memory subsets in PD-1+CD8+ T cells are related to clinical outcome. Specifically, baseline proportions of Tcm positively correlate with post-treatment proliferation, as indicated by elevated Ki-67 expression in PD-1+CD8+ T cells, while Tem exhibit a negative correlation with the increase of TIGIT+/PD-1+CD8+ T cells [77]. These dynamic changes imply that monitoring CD8+ T cells in peripheral blood could serve as a non-invasive biomarker for predicting clinical outcomes.

When combined, ICIs and chemotherapy also exert anti-tumor effects that are greater than those of either alone. The remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment by chemotherapy, together with the T-cell function-specific activation by ICIs, explains this enhancement. In individuals with relapsed or refractory acute myeloid leukemia, pembrolizumab and decitabine lead to clonal expansion of CD8+ Tem with activation and cytotoxic signatures [78]. When solid tumors were treated with nab-paclitaxel and pembrolizumab, pre-therapy and post-therapy tumor biopsies from responsive triple-negative breast cancer patients showed a reduction in populations of PD-1-high-expressing T cells. This treatment was also associated with increased Trm presence [79]. Moreover, when pembrolizumab was administered alongside metronomic cyclophosphamide for metastatic breast cancer, patients exhibiting clinical efficacy demonstrated a significant increase in CD4+/CD8+ T cell polyfunctionality, which lasted over one year in patients with complete remission [80]. Furthermore, patients with advanced gastric cancer who received sintilimab plus capecitabine and oxaliplatin chemotherapy had a greater percentage of PD-1+CD8+ memory T cells and an increased ratio of PD-1+CD8+ to PD-1+CD4+ T cells among patients responding to therapy [81]. In these responsive patients, the expression levels of PD-1 in CD4+ Tn, Tm, and Tcm also significantly increased [82]. The immunological markers were found to correlate with better PFS and overall survival, suggesting predictive value. The results of the above indicate that the combination of ICIs with chemotherapy can work synergistically to reshape the phenotype, function, and distribution patterns of memory T cells. Moreover, these combination regimens of ICIs with radio-therapy or particular molecular targeted therapy produce similar synergistic effects on reshaping aging memory T cell repertoire [[83], [84], [85], [86]], which demonstrates universal applicability of the strategies to modulate host immune status through combination therapy. In contrast to monotherapy, combination strategies have the potential to alter the memory T-cell pool more broadly, rendering them more suitable for in vivo CAR-T preconditioning.

sec.title: Molecular mechanisms of ICI-mediated reshaping and future directions
sec.p: As described in the previous sections, ICIs’ combination strategies exert synergistic regulation on memory T cell subsets. Nonetheless, the important molecular signalling pathways quantitatively relevant to such distinctive traits have not been evaluated systematically. Accumulating knowledge about these mechanisms can aid the conversion of empirical observations into predictable and modifiable pretreatment strategies. Given current fundamental immunological knowledge, the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (Akt)/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway has emerged as a central regulator of T cell metabolism and memory formation [87]. Mitochondrial injury due to chemotherapy may disrupt signaling pathways essential for memory T-cell development [47]. At the same time, immunometabolism research has shown a strong link between T cell differentiation states and metabolic patterns: memory T cells mainly use oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid oxidation, while Teff predominantly use glycolysis [88]. Chemotherapeutic agents can indirectly alter memory T cell formation by affecting their mitochondrial status and metabolic signaling [47]. Nevertheless, the regulatory associations between these metabolic alterations and upstream signaling pathways must be clarified.

Chemotherapy-induced immunogenic cell death releases tumor antigens and damage-associated molecular patterns, which promote dendritic cell maturation and antigen cross-presentation. This process lays the foundation for the expansion of specific memory T cells during the T cell priming phase [7,8,89]. When combined with ICIs, they can simultaneously eliminate the interference of co-inhibitory signals during the T cell priming phase, thereby further enhancing this priming effect [76,90]. In addition, the clearance of immunosuppressive populations by chemotherapy creates favorable conditions for the survival and expansion of memory T cells [[91], [92], [93], [94]]. Some chemotherapeutic agents, such as decitabine, possess epigenetic regulatory activity and can induce T cell differentiation to stem-like memory phenotypes through DNA demethylation and so on [95]. When combined with ICIs, they may synergistically prevent the establishment of exhaustion-associated epigenetic marks, allowing T cells to keep a state of low differentiation and high plasticity over a prolonged period.

It is essential to stress that the majority of the above mechanisms rest on indirect inferences from basic immunology, preclinical models, or correlational analyses; there is a paucity of high-quality mechanistic studies directly from clinical patient samples. Technologies like single-cell multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics, and in vivo lineage tracing will need to be used in the future to systematically map the evolutionary paths of immune subsets from combination therapy and identify the major molecular drivers involved [[96], [97], [98]]. This will enable the correlation of signaling pathway activity with T-cell phenotypes, functions, and clinical outcome to establish an important theoretical basis for optimizing in vivo CAR-T preconditioning.

sec.title: Heterogeneity in clinical responses to combination therapy: current status and critical reflections
sec.p: The last section explained how combination therapies synergistically regulate the memory T cells. However, there is substantial intertumour response variability in clinical efficacy across tumor type, patient population, and even studies of these combination regimens. To rationally design combination strategies and improve precision immunotherapy, the underlying causes of these differences should be thoroughly examined.

Tumor type-specific immune microenvironment differences account for the inconsistency in clinical responses [99]. Hematologic tumors and solid tumors are fundamentally different in their immune microenvironments, which impact the mobilization of memory T cells through combination therapies [99]. In case of hematologic tumors, malignant cells are found in the blood, lymphoid organs, and bone marrow. This makes T cells able to access tumor antigen easily. As a result of combinatorial therapies, the expansion of memory T cells is likely more direct and stronger in these cancers [99]. Solid tumors, on the other hand, present unique challenges. T cells must navigate the complex physical barriers of the tumor stroma. In addition, they must also contend with the effects of hypoxia, acidity, and competing metabolism within the tumor. All of this is necessary to reach the tumors and carry out effector functions there [99,100]. Even though combination therapies can expand memory T cells in the peripheral blood, the infiltration of such cells into the tumor microenvironment and their functional maintenance is challenging. This might explain the weak correlations found in studies on solid tumors between increased proportions of peripheral memory T cells and clinical effect [[100], [101], [102]].

It should not be forgotten that patients have heterogeneous baseline characteristics. The effectiveness of combination therapy relies greatly on the patient's initial immune status. Factors such as prior treatment history, the initial composition of the T-cell repertoire, age, and tumor burden can lead to significant variations in responses to the same combination regimen among different patients [5,59,[103], [104], [105]]. Consider the scenario of patients with severely exhausted T cells after multiple lines of therapy. Even theoretically optimized combination regimens may fail to elicit memory T-cell responses due, most likely, to an insufficient “cellular substrate [59].” Hence, the frequent absence in current trials of stratified analyses based on these baseline characteristics may explain inconsistent findings.

The heterogeneity of clinical outcomes is exacerbated by the inherent complexity of combinations. The ultimate efficacy may be affected by the choice of the chemotherapeutic agent, dose, administration sequence, and synergistic strategies with ICIs, among other factors; yet, systematic head-to-head comparative studies are lacking. As was described in Section 3.4, the dose-response relationship between chemotherapy and immunoregulation is nonlinear [44,55]. There is currently no agreement on how to choose an optimal dosage window when combining with ICIs to achieve the best balance between “relieving immunosuppression” and “preserving effector functions”. Furthermore, when to administer ICI (concurrent, sequential, and maintenance) will significantly determine its immunomodulatory effects [106]. The combination regimens in existing trials varied significantly, making comparison between trials and meta-analysis problematic.

Furthermore, in the absence of evaluation criteria, interpreting the results strain. Studies vary in definition and indicators for detecting the so-called “immune synergistic effects.” Some studies use changes in peripheral blood memory T cells as the main immunologic endpoint [104], while others cite phenotypic change of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes as the main indicator [107]. In addition, some investigations focus on T cell function or clonal diversity of T cell receptors, and there is no consensus on the standard of time points for detection [108]. So, there may be considerably different conclusions regarding the same combination therapy regimen due to these differences.

In conclusion, the clinical responses observed with ICIs combination therapies are often inconsistent due to a complex interplay of multiple factors such as tumor type, patient baseline characteristics, regimen design, and evaluation criteria. The current evidence is inadequate to support universal predictive models or uniform clinical guidelines.

sec.title: Implications for CAR-T cell therapy: from bench to bedside
The detrimental impact of chemotherapy on T cells and clinical implications
sec.p: As stated before, chemotherapy significantly impairs T cell fitness, which severely restricts the ability to harvest high-quality T cells from patients for in vitro expansion. This limitation is a critical factor in determining whether cancer patients, particularly those with solid tumors, can undergo CAR-T therapy [5,6].

Among the various chemotherapeutic agents, bendamustine has emerged as a significant risk factor for CAR-T manufacturing failure [53]. Repeated studies indicate that exposure to bendamustine results in a low peripheral blood platelet count, low CD4/CD8 ratios, and a high proportion of T cells expressing markers of exhaustion [53,54,109]. Another multi-centre study showed that patients were at risk of manufacturing failure when they received 3 or more cycles with less than a 3-month washout period and 6 or more cycles with a 3 to 24-month washout period [53]. Low platelet counts and low CD4/CD8 ratios (below 1:3) in the peripheral blood during the apheresis were independently associated with manufacturing failure [53]. Thus, the recommendation is to stop treatment with bendamustine prior to collection for 6 months and evaluation of both CD4/CD8 ratios and platelet count. It is interesting to note that the negative effects of bendamustine are more influenced by the time of recent exposure (e.g., nine months before apheresis) than by the “cumulative” dose [54]. The underlying mechanism for these negative effects may be attributed to chemotherapy-induced transcriptional and epigenetic shifts that promote an exhausted phenotype in T cells, which directly impairs the performance of CAR-T cell products derived after chemotherapy [32,50,51]. Consequently, these findings collectively emphasize the importance of collecting and cryopreserving T cells during the early stages of disease or before chemotherapy, offering critical insights for optimizing cell therapy strategies and addressing the raw material crisis induced by chemotherapy.

sec.title: The paramount importance of memory phenotypes
sec.p: Memory T cells, mainly the less-differentiated subsets, are important determinants of in vivo expansion potential, persistence, and clinical outcome of infused CAR-T products [4,58]. In terms of tumor clearance and long-lasting immune memory, CAR-T cells generated from Tcm or Tn/Tscm outperform CAR-T cells derived from Tem or terminally differentiated effector cells. Tcm cells survive longer in vivo and generate stronger, more sustained anti-leukemic responses [110]. Unlike Tem cells that secrete a lot of cytokines, have a shorter lifespan, and show reduced long-term effectiveness, they are associated with product expansion failure and toxicity [58,110,111]. Extensive clinical studies have confirmed a significant correlation between the high proportion of Tscm and Tcm in the final CAR-T product and superior long-term antitumor activity and patient survival [58,112]. More importantly, both the initial phenotype observed at apheresis and the cellular composition of the infusion product itself are determinants of treatment outcomes. Products with a higher proportion of Tcm cells are associated with prolonged in vivo persistence and sustained anti-leukemic responses, whereas products dominated by Teff often exhibit limited therapeutic efficacy [58,113,114]. In the context of CD19 CAR-T therapy for B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) and B-NHL, CAR-T products from patients who achieve complete remission (CR) not only demonstrate stronger expansion capacity and higher proportions of Tscm, but also show transcriptional enrichment of memory-associated gene signatures, such as the interleukin-6 (IL-6)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) pathway. In contrast, the cells of non-responders upregulate programs related to effector differentiation, exhaustion, and apoptosis [111]. Based on this discovery, CAR-T cell products enriched with Tn/Tscm have demonstrated remarkable response rates and sustained efficacy in adult patients with relapsed/refractory B-ALL (r/r B-ALL) and relapsed/refractory NHL (r/r NHL) [115,116]. Moreover, the functional complementarity and balance between CD4+ and CD8+ CAR-T cell subsets are critical for achieving optimal therapeutic outcomes [117,118]. Inclusion of the ratio of subsets, for instance, the ratio of 1:1 in the infusion product and memory phenotypes like CD8+ Tcm [111,117,119,120], allows in vivo expansion and sustained anti-tumor activity.

The latest study conducted a large-scale integrated analysis of 256 adult patients, encompassing five major hematologic malignancies: chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), multiple myeloma (MM), B-ALL, NHL, and acute myeloid leukemia. The conclusion was further validated with a study of more than two million apheresis-derived T cells [4]. The study indicates a higher proportion of naïve-like T cells in apheresis-derived T cells associated with enhanced CAR-T efficacy. In particular, the CD8+CD27+CD45RO− (±CCR7+CD28+) naïve-like T cell subset represents a central marker for a favorable outcome, while CD4+CD27+CD45RO+PD1+ central memory-like T cells are significantly associated with unfavorable outcome, especially pronounced in patients with CLL [4]. Xu et al. observed a significant correlation between the frequency of CD8+CD45RA+CCR7+ T cells characterized by the Tscm phenotype and the overall expansion of CAR-T cells in lymphoma patients. Moreover, a high fraction of CD8+ Tn cells in pre-treatment samples was identified as a potential predictor for superior in vivo expansion [121]. It is worth noting that this principle is applicable in solid tumor therapy, too. During Phase I trials, the infusion of Tcm-enriched epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) CAR-T products enhanced clinical responses in patients with metastatic prostate cancer, with stronger clinical responses correlating with the enrichment level of Tcm [102]. In a similar vein, Tcm-enriched EGFR CAR-T for advanced cholangiocarcinoma was found safe and effective, improving the prognosis of patients [100]. Additionally, the clinical efficacy and sustained response of disialoganglioside (GD2) CAR-T cells in high-risk neuroblastoma studies were closely linked to the proportion of CD4+ T cells and central memory cells present in the infusion product [101], thereby further emphasizing the significance of cell product quality.

CAR-T cells arising from early memory subpopulations, including Tn, Tscm, and Tcm, have been the bedrock of therapeutic efficacy owing to their improved in vivo expansion and persistence, as is collectively shown by results. This principle not only applies to hematologic malignancies but also has basic importance in overcoming solid tumor hurdles [[100], [101], [102],122], further underscoring the high significance of memory phenotype maintenance and enhancement in therapies.

sec.title: Challenges and strategies in CAR-T manufacturing: from T cell scarcity to innovative solutions
sec.p: The primary barriers to CAR-T manufacturing for patients with advanced malignancies, particularly those who are on high-intensity chemotherapy, are low T cell quantity and quality. Manufacturing failure or the inability to produce cell products with quality standards may reach up to 3.8% of all manufactured products [1]. The main causes include low cell viability, abnormal interferon-γ secretion, insufficient T cell purity, and low chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) transduction efficiency—all of which are closely related to the functional status of the patient's T cells [1,3,4]. In addition, as discussed in Section 5.1, factors such as a history of bendamustine use, low platelet counts, and a low CD4/CD8 ratio during apheresis are significantly associated with treatment failure [53,123]. In most chemotherapy regimens, however, the in vitro responsiveness of T cells to stimulation decreases with increasing cycles of chemotherapy. Older patients and those with solid tumors on high-intensity chemotherapy are particularly affected. T cell damage is more pronounced in these patients [5], which makes them less applicable to CAR-T therapy.

This initial composition of the T-cell repertoire is driven by intrinsic patient factors and the type of disease, leading to considerable differences in the expansion capabilities of T cells from various cancer patients in in vitro culture [4,13,104]. Research on childhood cancers showed that patients with SR-ALL, who are usually younger, have T-cell repertoires that are enriched for Tn and Tscm, signifying strong in vitro expansion potential. People who have NHL are older patients who frequently present with lymphopenia. In these patients, the T-cell compartments at diagnosis are characterized by early lineage cell exhaustion in a context of a dominance of highly-differentiated memory and effector cells, which inherently leads to a compromised capacity to expand [5,58,103]. Even among patients with ALL, high-risk patients show a pronounced decline in T-cell expansion capacity following intensive chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide and cytarabine, which is closely related to drug-selective depletion of Tn cells. Moreover, the disease stage majorly affects T cell quality. Indeed, T cells extracted from early-stage MM patients have significantly superior quality than cells derived from relapsed or refractory patients [58,124]. Moreover, the legacy effects of different chemotherapy regimens further emphasize the important role of past treatments on T-cell fitness. This means that, specifically, a lower exposure to immunomodulatory drugs (IMiDs) is favorably associated with higher levels of CCR7+CD8+ T cells and lower PD-1 expression [53,59]. Further, treatment with bendamustine leads to less favorable immune phenotypes, like a lower CD4/CD8 ratio along with higher levels of exhaustion markers [53,59].

Recognizing this heterogeneity presents opportunities for interventions aimed at enhancing manufacturing outcomes. The use of exogenous cytokines, for example, interleukin-7 (IL-7) and interleukin-15 (IL-15), during the manufacture has been shown to greatly enhance T cell proliferation and enrich the Tscm subset, which partially restores the expansion potential of T cells from patients with lymphoma, etc [5,58]. A more proactive approach is to collect and cryopreserve peripheral blood T cells at the onset of the disease or diagnosis for patients with rapidly progressive disease who are likely to suffer from apheresis. According to Palen et al., an early collection strategy is feasible for cells from healthy donors. This method only needs a small amount of peripheral blood (about 50 mL), from which peripheral blood mononuclear cells are isolated and cryopreserved [125]. This method allows for the production of enough CAR-T cell products in a short time frame. The cells collected by this strategy contain a lot of naïve or stem cell-like memory T cells with the CD45RA+CCR7+ phenotype. These T cells can significantly expand and last for a long time, allowing for the rapid manufacturing of high-quality CAR-T products [125]. This underscores the significance of early collection and cryopreservation of high-quality T cells during the initial treatment phase or when conditions are favorable, thus preserving valuable “seed” cells for subsequent successful cell therapy [[125], [126], [127]].

sec.title: From biomarkers to clinical decisions: detection and application of T cell phenotypes
Identification and detection of T cell phenotypes
sec.p: Since memory phenotype is central, the composition of pre-treated T cells (especially the presence of early differentiated subsets and exhaustion markers) is a strong predictor of CAR-T clinical outcomes [4,104,128]. This property has been validated in BCMA CAR-T treatment for MM. A phase I study revealed that patients with PFS of 18 months or longer exhibited higher numbers of Tn and lower levels of exhaustion markers in their apheresis products, alongside improved functional T cell phenotypes in the infusion products [114]. Analysis of the apheresis samples further revealed significantly higher CD8+ Tn/Tscm (CCR7+CD45RO−) and Tcm (CCR7+CD45RO+) proportions in the long-responder group (PFS >180 days). When evaluating CCR7+CD8+ T cells together, patients with a higher frequency of this phenotype had a longer PFS [59]. Long-responders received fewer doses of IMiDs before plasmapheresis, indicating that prior IMiDs exposures are associated with favorable long-term clinical outcomes and T-cell phenotypes [59]. In CD19 CAR-T therapies, high early-response rates are often associated with increased CD8+ Tn or Tscm proportions [6,129].

Stem cell-like memory T cells, being the least differentiated subset of memory T cells, exhibit dual phenotypic features of Tn and memory T cells. The criteria for identification are based on the combined analysis of the markers CD45RA+, CCR7+, CD27+, CD28+, CD95+, and CD122+. Various markers such as CD45RA+, CCR7+, CD62L+, CD27+, and CD28+ indicate a low differentiation state analogous to Tn [130,131]. The phenotypic identification of Tcm is relatively well-established and is typically defined as CD45RA−CCR7+CD62L+CD27+CD28+. While maintaining lymph node homing receptors, Tcm have lost CD45RA expression as compared to Tscm [11,130,132]. This retention gives them the ability to migrate to secondary lymphoid organs and a strong proliferative capacity.

The detection of the aforementioned phenotype is technically feasible [4,13,128]. Specifically, multicolor flow cytometry, the most commonly employed technique in clinical immune monitoring, can simultaneously detect 8 to 12 parameters, which is adequate to encompass the essential marker combinations for Tscm and Tcm [4]. The major T cell subsets, namely Tn, Tscm, Tcm, and Tem, can be fully identified using a nine-colour panel containing CD3, CD4, CD8, CD45RA, CCR7, CD62L, CD95, CD27, and CD28 [11,130,132]. Increasing the parameters and conducting mass cytometry or full-spectrum flow cytometry further integrates functional markers and detection of cytokines for mechanistic studies. However, the application of these tests in routine clinical practice still faces numerous challenges, including inadequate standardization, dilemmas regarding testing timing and sample selection, stability issues of rare subpopulations, and factors such as cost and accessibility. This underscores the need for establishing standardized operating procedures and automated analysis tools.

sec.title: Clinical application pathways of T cell phenotypes
sec.p: The implementation of T-cell phenotyping within the overall workflow of CAR-T therapy at the level of clinical practice should follow a refined technical pathway. It is advisable to perform multiparameter flow cytometry analysis of peripheral blood T cells before apheresis to evaluate absolute counts and relative proportions of key memory subsets in the pre-treatment screening phase [4,104]. Patients with much reduced Tn or Tscm proportions or who overexpress exhaustion markers should be considered a “high-risk” population for CAR-T manufacturing failure or suboptimal efficacy [53,59]. For the patients, a rigorous assessment of the practicality of proceeding with autologous CAR-T therapy should be carried out, or a more aggressive design of preconditioning regimens should be considered. T-cell phenotype testing results can be beneficial in establishing individualized preconditioning regimens [5]. An inventive approach might involve using the standard lymphodepleting chemotherapy for those patients with baseline memory T-cell pools relatively intact for the generation of immune space and for increasing levels of homeostatic cytokines. On the other hand, patients with considerable baseline memory T-cell exhaustion or naïve lineage depletion require selective optimization of the preconditioning regimen. This means they can't use drugs with long-term T-cell toxicities (bendamustine, for example) [53,54,109], especially in those recently exposed. Also, a preferential selection of preconditioning agents with immunomodulatory potential has to be carried out [59]. For patients with prominent exhausted phenotypes, it is worth considering incorporating ICIs into the lymphodepletion regimen to prevent T-cell suppression and enhance subsequent CAR-T cell in vivo expansion and functional persistence [90,133]. It is better to set up a mechanism for continuous monitoring during the treatment [4,104]. If the proportion of memory T cells shows a predicted rebound after lymphodepletion, pretreatment effectiveness was likely good. Alternatively, one needs to be on the lookout for potential combination treatments that are not performing optimally if the proportion is always low or a more severe exhaustion phenotype. In such situations, the options may include delaying the administration, lowering the dosage, or providing salvage therapy. To summarize, the transition of T-cell phenotypes from retrospective prognostic biomarkers into prospective clinical decision-making tools is an important milestone for personalized and precise CAR-T therapy [4].

sec.title: The ultimate challenge: patients with end-stage T cell exhaustion after multi-line therapy
sec.p: The preceding sections have systematically elucidated the cumulative T cell exhaustion induced by chemotherapy and its detrimental effects on CAR-T efficacy. In reality, clinical practice often deals with significantly tougher patients who continue to progress due to treatment (high-intensity chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapy, etc). In addition, the T cell function of patients in this cohort is severely exhausted. These patients typically exhibit the following characteristics: low absolute lymphocyte counts in peripheral blood that are persistently below the lower limit of normal; a near lack of Tn or Tscm; high expression of multiple exhaustion markers in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, including PD-1, T cell immunoglobulin and mucin-domain-containing-3 (TIM-3) and lymphocyte activation gene-3 (LAG-3); decreased basal OCR and SRC, indicating impaired mitochondrial quality and function; very low proliferative potential upon in vitro stimulation; and sensitivity to AICD [5,32,47,104].

For these extreme patients, conventional autologous CAR-T therapy can't be used as the T cells collected via apheresis are both inadequate in number and substantially poor in quality, leading to extremely high rates of failure during in vitro manufacturing [1,2,53]. Even when successful production occurs, the end product consists mainly of terminally differentiated effector cells, which have a major deficit of memory subsets. This deficiency ultimately results in a poor capacity for expansion in vivo as well as short post-infusion persistence and very limited clinical benefits [1,2,53]. This is one of the main reasons why current CAR-T therapy is not efficacious in patients with solid tumors and heavily pre-treated hematologic malignancies.

The suggestion of a CAR-T strategy in vivo presents a new approach to solving this problem. Its primary advantage lies in its ability to directly utilize residual, even extremely limited, high-quality T cell subsets within the host for in situ reprogramming, rather than relying on the collection of substantial quantities of high-quality T cells from patients for ex vivo expansion [134]. This strategy can solve the problem of severely exhausted patients from multiple dimensions. At the cellular source level, it may capitalize on residual memory cell potential. The peripheral blood and tissues of patients whose T cell repertoires are severely limited may still contain small numbers of Tscm or Tn. Via targeted delivery vectors, CAR genes can be delivered to rare yet high-quality cells for the expansion and further differentiation into functional CAR-T cells in vivo [135]. Moreover, the in vivo CAR-T strategy can mitigate the terminal differentiation and functional exhaustion of T cells frequently observed during conventional ex vivo manufacturing processes, thus better preserving the low differentiation state and memory potential of the cells. At the preconditioning level, we should integrate an optimized “immune restoration” approach with lymphodepletion for severely depleted patients. For example, before launching the in vivo CAR-T infusion, coadministering a low dose of ICIs (such as anti-PD-1/PD-L1) could partially reverse the exhaustion state of endogenous T cells and thus provide a functionally superior “substrate” for subsequent transfection [90]. Immunomodulators (e.g., IMiDs) may alternatively be used to enrich residual memory T cells [59]. The combination of cytokines (interleukin-2 [IL-2], IL-6, IL-7, IL-15) can also be considered as a way to transiently induce the survival and proliferation potential of residual T cells [58,136,137].

It must be emphasized that the in vivo CAR-T strategy for severe T-cell exhaustion patients is presently only being studied theoretically and preclinically. This requires dedicated clinical trials in the future to evaluate the feasibility. In other words, the in vivo CAR-T strategy holds significant translational medical value specifically for severely exhausted T-cell patients who are resistant to conventional therapies. It provides new hope for completely hopeless patients facing “no treatment options” and “no useable cells,” but it is more demanding for researchers technically.

sec.title: In vivo CAR-T: principles and promise
sec.p: Several important bottlenecks exist that limit the widespread application of current autologous CAR-T therapies owing to complex manufacturing processes, high costs, long duration of production, and uncontrollable quality of starting T cells [138]. More critically, the in vitro manufacturing process exacerbates terminal differentiation and functional exhaustion of T cells, which is particularly damaging to memory T cell subsets, such as Tscm and Tcm, that can provide long-lasting therapeutic benefit [139,140].

The in vivo CAR-T strategy aims to fundamentally overcome the abovementioned bottlenecks through an “in-situ reprogramming” approach. The main idea behind the technology is to genetically modify circulating T cells in the patient's body through the intravenous infusion of vectors, which enables the generation of CAR-T cells in vivo in a one-step process [134,141]. This approach offers three game-changing benefits compared to the traditional methods. Firstly, this method eases the generation of functional CAR-T cells within 1-2 days due to the absence of complex ex vivo manipulations, thus reducing costs and patient waiting time significantly [142]. Secondly, this tactic successfully avoids cell exhaustion linked with manufacturing. Because reprogramming takes place in the natural microenvironment of somatic cells, it is likely to better preserve the memory phenotype and proliferation potential of T cells at their source, thus yielding more persistent products. The clinical translation of this strategy has recently made important advancements. Wang and co-workers used messenger RNA (mRNA)-lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based in vivo CD19 CAR-T cell therapy in five patients with refractory systemic lupus erythematosus. This research indicated that the treatment could accelerate functional CAR-T cell generation in vivo, eliminate B cells, improve disease conditions, and maintain controllable safety [134].

The translation of in vivo CAR-T therapy to humans continues to face several key hurdles. Clinical translation must comprehensively address issues such as the accurate targeting of vector design, off-target modification risk, safety control of in vivo gene delivery, and process translation obstacles of “off-the-shelf” products [141]. Among them, the translation of production processes stands out in particular: the good manufacturing practice (GMP)-level manufacture and the need for batch-to-batch consistency in parameters such as vector size, charge, and encapsulation efficiency [143]. Similarly, complex remains large-scale production. In addition, differences in immune systems between animal models and humans complicate dose translation for clinical applications. Taking all these into consideration, collectively, these present a substantial technical hurdle for the stable and effective targeting of memory T cells. The clinical translation of any advanced therapy medicinal product must ensure a stringent control of the risk of off-target effects, cytokine release syndrome, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, insertional mutations, and immunogenicity due to viral and non-viral vectors [[144], [145], [146]]. These safety concerns represent distinct research domains in vector design, gene editing, and immunopharmacology, and systematic reviews have been conducted to consolidate the existing knowledge in these areas [[144], [145], [146]].

While prioritizing safety, the in vivo CAR-T strategy reveals multiple optimization pathways across technical dimensions within the “off-the-shelf” framework from a long-term developmental perspective. When it comes to safety, the non-integrating vectors, like mRNA-LNP, offer significant benefits for patients receiving multiple therapies. Non-integrating vectors, therefore, completely remove the risk of insertional mutagenesis for patients with a high level of genomic instability [141]. CAR-T cells administered through mRNA have limited persistence but can have clinical use as a bridging therapy before transplant or as “immune priming” [134]. As far as universality is concerned, using vectors that target universal T cell surface markers allows for the direct reprogramming of all T cells in the patient, including less exhausted ones, without relying on the quality of autologous T cells [135]. This solution circumvents issues associated with T cell quality. In theory, this addresses the constraints of individualized production; however, off-target effects and immune compatibility must be evaluated for risk. These innovations enable successful CAR-T therapies, offering innovative solutions to vital production constraints and expanding the application of CAR-T therapies in clinical settings [[144], [145], [146]]. More significantly, their true potential lies in transforming traditional therapeutic approaches into proactive “host preconditioning” strategies. This method systematically enhances the baseline state of the endogenous T-cell repertoire, thereby establishing superior “cellular substrates” and a favorable immune microenvironment for in vivo CAR-T therapy.

sec.title: Key challenge: targeting and enriching memory T cells
sec.p: The challenge in question is transfecting high-quality T cells provided by the host, specifically those that belong to the memory T cell subsets. This will help in enhancing the in vivo generated CAR-T products and also enable the utilization of the endogenous T cell repertoire of high quality. By designing vectors that target specific surface markers, such as CD62L, to actively enrich and transfect the host's natural Tn/Tscm, along with other high-quality memory T cell subsets to enhance product quality from source [135].

The biggest challenge that needs to be overcome is to ensure that the vector can recognize and transfect specific T-cell subsets efficiently. It is critical to prevent, where possible, the unintentional transduction of non-target cells such as hepatocytes, macrophages, monocytes, or tumor cells, which may induce unwanted masking of epitopes, off-target effects, or engineering of unwanted immunosuppressive cells [142]. A major challenge in this regard is the selective targeting of memory T-cell subsets expressing CD62L+ or CCR7+. Of particular concern is the risk of inadvertent transfection of inhibitory cells, such as Tregs, which would not only fail to achieve therapeutic effects but might also exacerbate immune suppression and worsen the tumor microenvironment [144,146,147]. Currently, researchers are trying to solve this problem using a range of methods. One of which is modifying the envelope proteins of viral vectors so that they are able to recognize memory T cell surface markers [135]. Another method involves conjugating targeting antibodies or ligands to the surfaces of lipid nanoparticles [[148], [149], [150]]. Even with successful transfection of target T cells, the constitutive expression of CAR molecules on the cellular surface will induce persistent tonic signaling [151], ultimately resulting in antigen-independent T cell exhaustion and impaired in vivo persistence.

While the aforementioned challenges emphasize “precise identification” and “post-transfection effects,” the safety of the delivery technology itself must not be overlooked [[144], [145], [146]]. Therefore, generating CAR-T cells enriched with memory phenotypes efficiently and safely will enhance the in vivo persistence of CAR-T therapy.

sec.title: Towards in vivo CAR-T: transforming chemotherapy and ICI into host pre-conditioning strategies
Pre-conditioning value of chemotherapy and ICI
sec.p: The success of in vivo CAR-T strategies critically depends on our ability to actively shape an “in vivo production workshop” enriched with high-quality memory T cells. Chemotherapy and ICIs are important host preconditioning strategies that contribute to enhancing the baseline state of the endogenous T cell repertoire. As explained in Sections 3, 4, chemotherapy, by means of lymphodepletion, creates “ecological niches” for the expansion of CAR-T cells while also eliminating immunosuppressive populations such as Tregs and MDSCs [91,93]. This treatment induces the immunogenic cell death that stimulates antigen release and cross-presentation [152,153]. Lymphodepletion can boost IL-7 and IL-15 [92,94], which can create a conducive immune environment for in vivo CAR-T cells generation and expansion. In contrast, ICIs mitigate intrinsic T cell immunoinhibition by interfering with the exhaustion phenotype [90,133]. This results in a shift in the memory T cell pool, creating a better and more superior “cellular substrate” for the in vivo CAR-T cells. The synergistic effects of these mechanisms collectively aim to proactively shape an immune environment rich in functional memory T cells before the generation of in vivo CAR-T cells.

sec.title: Integrating pre-conditioning into in vivo CAR-T workflow
sec.p: The rational design of the drug administration sequence in combination therapy is crucial for determining the optimal integration sequence of chemotherapy and ICIs. This makes the rational design of a drug administration sequence very important. The time of chemotherapy as a pretreatment strategy is well-established and should occur before the in vivo CAR-T administration. This strategy focuses on fulfilling several purposes at once, such as lymphodepletion, elimination of immunosuppressive cells, upregulation of homeostatic cytokines, and optimization of T cell repertoire. The most important thing is the selection of the right chemotherapy regimen and intensity that achieves a favorable balance between immunostimulation and immunosuppression [7].

In comparison, the timing strategy of ICIs is more complex and variable, which provides multiple options for in vivo CAR-T therapy. A commonly used method administers ICI after CAR-T infusion in order to relieve the inhibition of CAR-T cells within the tumor microenvironment that may show early exhaustion after migrating there. Clinical trials have demonstrated that the use of pembrolizumab following CD19 CAR-T infusion is safe for patients with refractory or relapsed B-cell lymphoma and can facilitate CAR-T cell expansion while inducing clinical responses [90]. Another study highlighted the importance of the timing of ICI initiation: the administration of durvalumab before CAR-T infusion was associated with inferior efficacy, characterized by a slower accumulation of CAR-T cells and reduced levels of inflammatory cytokines. However, continued administration of durvalumab post-infusion resulted in observable CAR-T cell re-expansion and an extended duration of response [106]. Faced with this complexity, the “ready-to-use” design internalizes the mechanism of action of ICIs within the CAR-T system itself, enabling CAR-T cells to autonomously acquire resistance to inhibitory signals, thereby effectively eliminating the challenge associated with the timing of exogenous drug administration [154,155]. The core of this design concept is the integration of anti-exhaustion functions, such as the encoding of PD-1 blocking elements, into the delivery vector through genetic engineering strategies [126,154,156].

sec.title: Preclinical and clinical support for combinatorial preconditioning
sec.p: There is a substantial amount of preclinical and clinical evidence supporting the potential of combination strategies in CAR-T therapy in vivo. According to the key findings, pre-treatment chemo regimens can modify the quality of T cell “raw materials”. For example, chemotherapy can increase the susceptibility of the tumor cells to killing [157], induce immune memory [158], and remodel the immune environment systemically. Neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX chemotherapy exemplifies this approach by reducing Treg cell frequency while increasing effector memory subsets in CD4/CD8+ T cells [159]. Additionally, decitabine promotes the expansion of stem-like CD8+ T cells in tumor-draining lymph nodes while enhancing the effector functions of exhaustion-like T cells within the tumor microenvironment [95]. When taken in sum, these findings suggest that chemotherapy may create favorable conditions for the in vivo generation and expansion of CAR-T cells through the aforementioned mechanisms.

Regarding ICI, its synergistic effects provide dual strategic insights for overcoming the inhibitory microenvironment. Evidence indicates that anti-PD-1/PD-L1 antibodies can be combined with CAR-T therapy to produce significant synergistic effects [[160], [161], [162]], with the intensity of synergy depending on the costimulatory domains in the CAR construct and the T cell subsets utilized for CAR-T generation (e.g., Tcm-derived cells demonstrate heightened sensitivity). This effect is closely associated with the expression levels of the PD-1/PD-L1 axis in CAR-T cells [162]. Furthermore, endogenous engineering modifications have shown superior persistence and safety in clinical applications. CAR-T cells with PD-1 knockout or integrated PD-1 blocking elements exhibit significantly enhanced efficacy compared to conventional products [126,156], thereby providing a pathway for the design of in vivo CAR-T vectors. Furthermore, new targets beyond PD-1/PD-L1 are being developed. The blocking of the CD161-C-type lectin domain family 2 member D (CLEC2D) axis is reported to improve memory CD8+ T cell functionality in bone marrow and alleviate CAR-T exhaustion [163]. The leukocyte-associated Ig-like receptor 1 (LAIR1) targeting induces the shift of M2 macrophage towards M1 phenotype, enhances the memory T cell responses, and, combined with CAR-T, has a synergistic anti-tumor effect [164]. This provides potentially new insights into CAR-T therapy multi-target regulation in vivo.

In conclusion, chemotherapy and ICIs, as strategies for host preconditioning, can optimize the in vivo CAR-T immune environment and enhance cellular substrate quality through various mechanisms. These include reshaping the immune landscape, alleviating T-cell suppression, and facilitating endogenous engineering. Future studies should assess how these therapies can precisely regulate the endogenous T-cell repertoire, how to develop “multifunctional” vectors co-expressing immunomodulatory factors, and how to test out different combinatorial strategies in well-designed clinical trials, with the ultimate purpose of obtaining personalized in vivo CAR-T therapy.

sec.title: Conclusion and future perspectives
sec.p: This review systematically explains the beneficial or negative effects of chemotherapy and ICIs for the T-cell repertoire of cancer patients. It particularly focuses on Tn and Tscm cells crucial for establishing long-term immune memory. While these therapies might exacerbate T-cell exhaustion and alter differentiation, they can remodel the immune environment, providing an opportunity to improve the cellular substrate of the CAR-T cell therapy. Standard CAR-T therapy may suffer from sub-optimal T-cells isolated from the patient and bottlenecks in in vitro manufacturing. The in vivo CAR-T approach based on the revolutionary “in situ reprogramming” strategy will be the definite way forward for next-generation cellular immunotherapy. The central thesis of this paper is that the efficacy of this strategy will depend not only on advancements in delivery technology but also on a fundamental change in the way therapies are conceived. This shift involves proactively transforming chemotherapy and ICIs from conventional treatment modalities into an active host preconditioning strategy. By actively optimizing the composition and functional quality of the endogenous T cell repertoire, we aim to establish an ideal “in vivo production workshop” for the efficient generation and sustained activity of CAR-T cells within the body.

The future of in vivo CAR-T therapy depends on synergistic exploration and paradigm innovation across multiple frontiers. Efforts were directed first of all to the development of precise individualized preconditioning strategies consisting of a systematic mapping of various regimens of chemotherapy and ICIs on the T-cell repertoires of patients with different immune subtypes of the disease. A combination with Tscm/Tcm phenotypes for patient stratification is achieved for personalized immune-tailored regimens. Another core pathway involves designing intelligent “off-the-shelf” delivery vectors that not only intrinsically evade T-cell exhaustion but also actively target and transfect high-quality subsets such as Tn/Tscm, fundamentally ensuring the quality of in vivo generated products. Meanwhile, the development of synthetic biology strategies has opened new avenues for achieving dynamic and tumor microenvironment-responsive regulation of CAR-T functions, including logic-gated CARs [[165], [166], [167]]. The synergistic application of these innovative designs with host preconditioning strategies warrants further in-depth exploration in the future.

In this context, the introduction of adaptive clinical trial design is essential. For disruptive technologies like in vivo CAR-T, the exploratory trial phase should specifically prioritize the integration of dose exploration with biomarker validation. Through constructing dose cohorts and monitoring the dynamic changes of T-cell subsets throughout the course of the disease cohort, we could integrate immune kinetic parameters, e.g., changes in peripheral blood Tscm/Tcm ratios, peak CAR-T cell levels in vivo, and CAR-T cell persistence into a composite endpoint. This method helps to quickly identify the best combination strategies. Furthermore, it enables the establishment of a correlation model between immune kinetics and clinical efficacy, providing scientific justification for dosage selection for subsequent confirmatory trials. Detection of T cell subsets with an ultra-sensitive T cell subset detection method for depleted patient populations and other special groups to accurately quantify and assess the function of residual memory T cells. The characteristics of these residual T cells must be used to build individualized treatment decision models to identify the patients who are most likely to respond to in vivo CAR-T therapy. At the same time, the therapeutic vision must shift from the cell product to the in vivo immune ecosystem. Future breakthroughs should prioritize the synergistic activation of the host's endogenous immune system, thereby transforming CAR-T therapy into an engine that triggers sustained immune responses. In conclusion, shifting the treatment paradigm away from “cell product manufacturing” and toward “in vivo immune environment shaping and activation” may improve the efficacy, durability, and accessibility of in vivo CAR-T therapy.
